Blue moki (Latridopsis ciliaris) attain a maximum recorded total length of approximately 80 cm [Li = approximately 80 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of the family Latridae in New Zealand waters. Field surveys and catch data from the Chatham Rise indicate that individuals exceeding this length are exceedingly rare, suggesting that 80 cm represents an asymptotic upper bound for somatic growth in this species. The relationship between length and mass is well described by a power-law function, with the ultimate wet weight corresponding to this maximum length reaching 8754 grams [Wwi = 8754 grams]. This considerable body mass is associated with a deep, laterally compressed body form that facilitates maneuverability in the rocky reef habitats they frequent. Comparative data from related teleosts suggest that such a large size confers advantages in terms of predator avoidance and competitive dominance for spawning sites, though it also entails a longer period of somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive activity.

Reproductive development in Latridopsis ciliaris is characterized by the attainment of sexual maturity at a standard length of 40 cm [Lp = 40 cm], a size typically reached after several years of sustained feeding in coastal environments. This length at puberty marks the transition from the juvenile to the adult phase, during which gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis commence. Field observations of gravid females indicate that individuals begin contributing to the spawning stock once they surpass this threshold, which corresponds roughly to half the ultimate total length. The delay in maturation until 40 cm is likely an adaptive response to the high energetic demands of gamete production in a species that produces large, pelagic eggs. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation is tightly linked to seasonal temperature cues, ensuring that spawning coincides with periods of optimal planktonic productivity for the resulting exogenously feeding larvae.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C], the embryonic development of Latridopsis ciliaris proceeds rapidly, with egg hatching occurring after 8 days [ab = 8 days]. This brief incubation period is characteristic of many temperate marine teleosts spawning in relatively warm waters and reflects a strategy of rapid yolk absorption by the developing embryo. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries an initial wet weight at birth of 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a diminutive mass that underscores the substantial maternal investment required for the production of a large number of small eggs. This weight, derived from an egg diameter of approximately 1.3 mm, is consistent with values reported for the congeneric species Latris lineata. The transition from lecithotrophy to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after eclosion, with the timing of first prey capture being critical for larval survival.

The maximum reproductive rate documented for Latridopsis ciliaris, observed at a water temperature of 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C], shows that females release approximately 2274 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2274 eggs per spawning event] and spawn approximately 365 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 times per year] during the peak of the spawning season. This daily output, calculated from life-history data of the closely related Latris lineata, is achieved through a combination of a high fecundity per spawning event and a sustained spawning frequency. The annual reproductive output is considerable, reflecting an iteroparous life-history strategy in which adults spawn multiple times over their lifespan. These values are not directly measured from captive trials but are inferred from fecundity-length relationships and spawning interval estimates derived from wild populations. Such a high rate of gamete release imposes substantial metabolic costs on reproductive females, requiring them to maintain high feeding rates to replenish somatic reserves during the breeding period.

Long-term tagging studies and otolith-based age estimates indicate that Latridopsis ciliaris exhibits a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 33 years [am = approximately 33 years] at 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C]. This exceptional longevity, unusual for a fast-growing temperate reef fish, positions the species as a relatively slow-living member of its guild, with a life-history strategy that prioritizes repeated reproduction across many seasons. The survival of adults over such an extended period is facilitated by their large body size and the relative stability of their deep reef habitats. In comparison to shorter-lived congeners, this extended lifespan allows for a greater cumulative reproductive output per individual, buffering the population against sporadic recruitment failures. The combination of a long lifespan, late maturity at 40 cm standard length, and high daily fecundity delineates a life-history pattern that is sensitive to overfishing, as the removal of older, more fecund individuals can profoundly impact population resilience.
